topic.about.title: About Phoenix MCP
topic.about.body:
Phoenix MCP lets AI agents work with your Home Assistant, safely. Each agent gets its own access key, and you decide what that key can see and do.

## Two ways to use it {#ways}

- **Agent Chat**: chat with an AI model right inside Home Assistant. You add an account with an AI provider, and Phoenix runs the agent for you.
- **An external app**: connect an MCP client, such as a desktop assistant or a coding tool, with an access key. The app's own model does the thinking.
- **Home Assistant's own assistants**: Phoenix can answer as a voice agent, run AI Task actions, or lend its tools to another assistant.

Either way, every action goes through the same checks, and the audit log records it.

Related: [{{label:agentchat.title}}](guide:window.agentChat), [Connecting External Apps](guide:topic.connecting), [Voice Agent, AI Task or Assist Tool Provider](guide:topic.homeAssistantFeatures)

## What every action goes through {#checks}

1. **Capabilities**: what kinds of things the key may do at all, such as control devices or edit automations. Each is Deny, Allow or Confirm.
2. **Permissions**: which areas, devices and entities the key can see and change.
3. **MESA**: how careful to be with each device, whatever the key allows: let agents act, ask you first, or keep them off it.
4. **Approvals**: an action set to Confirm waits until you approve it.

Related: [What Agents Can Do](guide:topic.tools), [Security](guide:topic.security), [{{label:accessKeys.cardCapabilities}}](guide:window.capabilities), [How a permission is decided](guide:topic.permissionResolution), [How MESA Decides](guide:topic.mesaRules), [How an approval works](guide:topic.approvalLifecycle)

## Why not a long-lived access token {#token}

A Home Assistant long-lived access token acts as your user, across all of Home Assistant's interfaces. Anything holding it can do what you can.

An access key works only with Phoenix. It has its own permissions and optional expiry, and a rate limit on Phoenix's own connection. You can revoke it without touching your own login. Phoenix's connection doesn't accept Home Assistant tokens.

## Where to start {#start}

In the {{label:shell.tabAccessKeys}} workspace, select **{{label:accessKeys.setUpAgent}}**. The setup walks you through a key, its permissions, and either Agent Chat or an external app, then lets you test the connection.

Related: [How your agent connects](guide:wizard.choose), [Installing Phoenix MCP](guide:topic.install)

topic.approvalLifecycle.title: How an Approval Works
topic.approvalLifecycle.body:
What happens to a request from the moment an agent asks until it's decided, and what the agent is told along the way.

## What waits for you {#held}

A capability set to Confirm holds the changes it covers. Reads covered by the same capability run straight away.

MESA's Confirm holds an action only while MESA is Enforced. One approval covers both, so you never approve the same action twice. Configuration recovery also asks here before it puts something back.

Related: [Deny, Allow and Confirm](guide:window.capabilities#modes)

## What the agent is told {#agent}

- External apps hear at once that the request is waiting, and can ask for the outcome later. With an [inline approval wait](guide:window.keySettings#inline-wait), the app waits up to that long for your decision first.
- Agent Chat waits for your decision for up to 15 minutes. If no decision comes by then, or the chat ends first, the request is cancelled.
- The Voice Agent, Assist and AI Task don't wait: they report that the change is waiting for approval and carry on. Approving later still runs it.

## How long a request waits {#expiry}

A pending request expires after one hour. Once it has, Review offers only Reject, and rejecting it records it as expired. Each access key can have up to 100 pending requests at once.

## What happens when you approve {#approve}

Phoenix checks the request again before running it:

- An expired request closes as expired.
- If the access key was revoked or has expired, the request is cancelled.
- If its capability is now Deny, the request fails without running.
- If the kill switch is on, the request is cancelled.

Phoenix then records your decision before it runs anything. Each action also checks its own targets, permissions and MESA rules again. If the devices it targets have changed since the request, it's refused, and the agent must ask again.

## How it can end {#outcomes}

- Approved: it ran, and its result is saved.
- Failed: it was refused at the last check, or the action returned an error. It isn't offered again.
- Interrupted: it stopped while running and may have partly applied. Check the result yourself.

Only a failure before the action starts leaves the request pending, to approve again.

## Rejecting {#reject}

The agent receives your reason, or is told to ask you if you gave none. A rejected configuration recovery keeps the current configuration.

## What ends a request early {#cancelled}

Restarting Home Assistant cancels every pending request. So do revoking its access key, the key expiring, and deleting core data. Approving while the kill switch is on cancels the request instead.

## Notifications {#notify}

With **{{label:settings.notifyApprovalLabel}}** on, each request raises a Home Assistant notification that links to it, and the notification goes away once the request is decided.

Related: [Home Assistant notifications](guide:window.settingsLogs#notify-approval)

## History {#history}

Decided requests are kept for seven days, up to the newest 500. Their arguments, change and result are cleared about an hour after the decision. Interrupted requests stay in the list, so you can check what happened, but their arguments, change and result are cleared after seven days too.

topic.commandRouting.title: How a Command Is Routed
topic.commandRouting.body:
Simple commands like "turn off the kitchen light" don't need a full AI model. When command handling is on, Phoenix tries cheaper ways first.

## The order Phoenix tries {#order}

1. Home Assistant's sentence matching, in every installed Assist language. It runs in your home and costs nothing.
2. The decision provider, if you use one. It handles the commands sentence matching missed.
3. Your AI model, for everything else, just as without command handling.

Once a step carries out a command, the later steps aren't used.

Related: [Decision provider](guide:window.settingsProviders#decision-provider)

## When it applies {#when}

You turn command handling on separately for [Agent Chat](guide:window.settingsChat#chat-commands) and the [Voice Agent](guide:window.settingsHome#voice-commands).

It only applies to plain text messages. Messages for Home Companion keys always go straight to the companion.

## Follow-up messages {#follow-ups}

The first message in a conversation can go to the decision provider. A follow-up only goes there with a TypeSafe / JEV model, in a language the model supports. Otherwise it goes to your AI model.

## Limits {#limits}

The decision provider has a time limit for each request, and an optional hourly limit. If either is reached, the command goes to your AI model, so nothing goes unanswered.

Related: [Connection settings](guide:window.settingsProviders#decision-connection)

## Seeing the effect {#effect}

Routing statistics count how each message was handled, so you can see what command handling saves you.

Related: [Reading the statistics](guide:topic.routingStatistics)

topic.configurationHistory.title: What Changes Records
topic.configurationHistory.body:
Phoenix records a change after an agent's write has succeeded, with the item before and after it. Changes approved in Approvals are recorded the same way; requests you reject record nothing.

## What is recorded {#recorded}

- Automations, scripts and scenes.
- Helpers, including zones, tags and people, and the settings of integration-based helpers.
- Dashboard layouts and the Energy dashboard.
- Blueprints.
- Entity and device registry edits, and integration names and options.
- Areas, floors, labels and categories.
- Restores from this panel, as rollbacks.

## What is not {#not-recorded}

Changes made outside Phoenix, in Home Assistant itself, aren't recorded. Neither are actions on devices, calendar events, to-do items, the dashboard list or dashboard resources.

Some records exist only as evidence and can't be restored, such as removing an integration or a device.

## How long it's kept {#retention}

Phoenix keeps the 20 newest changes to each item, with no time limit. History survives restarts. Deleting core data in [Data Management](guide:window.settingsSafety#wipe-core) clears it.

Records hold the configuration exactly as it was, so a restore can put it back. Only administrators can see them.

## What a restore can put back {#restore}

- Automations, scripts, scenes, helpers and blueprints: edited back, or recreated under their original ID if they were deleted.
- Dashboards: the layout is put back, but a deleted dashboard isn't recreated.
- Entities and devices: their names, areas, labels and similar registry details. A deleted entity can't be recreated.
- Areas, floors, labels and categories: only while the same item still exists.
- The Energy dashboard: its whole configuration.

Restoring a helper usually replaces it whole, so fields added since are removed. A configuration that used !secret, !include or similar tags can't be restored.

## Safety copies {#recovery}

Before some risky writes, Phoenix also keeps a safety copy, separate from Changes. If a write may not have finished, Phoenix asks in Approvals whether to put the copy back. Safety copies survive deleting core data.

topic.connecting.title: Connecting External Apps
topic.connecting.body:
An external app, such as a coding assistant or a desktop chat app, connects to Phoenix with one access key. The app's own model does the thinking, and Phoenix decides what it may do.

## Getting the setup commands {#commands}

Phoenix shows the exact command or configuration for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity CLI, Codex, Cursor and DeepSeek Harness, plus a general one for any other MCP app. They appear in three places:

- The **Connect** step of [{{label:accessKeys.setUpAgent}}](guide:wizard.connect).
- **{{label:accessKeys.postCreateConnectTitle}}**, right after you create a key.
- **{{label:accessKeys.helpConnect}}**, after you rotate a key.

The commands contain the key itself, which Phoenix shows only once. To see them again for an existing key, rotate it and update the app.

Each app's tab links to that app's own setup guide. Restart or reload the app afterwards.

## Keeping the key safe {#credentials}

The access key works like a password for everything its permissions allow. Phoenix stores only a fingerprint of it, so it can't show it again.

Keep it out of shared files and chat logs. The setup commands for Claude Code, Gemini and Codex put it on the command line, so clear your shell history if others can read it. If it leaks, [rotate](guide:window.accessKeys#rotate) the key: the old value stops working straight away.

## Using several keys {#several-keys}

Give each app or task its own key, with only the permissions it needs. Each key gets its own server name in the app, such as phx-home, so one app can hold several keys side by side.

Renaming a key keeps it working, but new setup commands use the new name.

## The connection {#connection}

Apps connect to your Home Assistant address followed by /api/phoenix-mcp, sending the key as a bearer token. The URL in the setup commands is the one your browser uses; change it there if the app reaches Home Assistant another way.

Phoenix speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP. Older app settings that use the SSE transport won't connect. Long actions keep the connection alive with a message every 15 seconds.

## When the tools change {#reconnect}

Some apps read the list of tools only when they connect. After you change a key's capabilities or permissions, reconnect the app to see the new list. Phoenix also tells the agent on its next call: to reconnect when its tools changed, or, when only which actions need approval changed, that its tools are the same.

Related: [Reconnecting an agent](guide:window.accessKeys#reconnect)

## What the agent is told {#primer}

When an app connects, Phoenix sends it short instructions for working safely: how approvals and dry runs work, which actions need your approval, and the key's notes. A Home Companion key gets a shorter fixed version.

Apps that support skills can also install the Phoenix MCP skill, a longer guide shown under **{{label:wizard.skillSectionTitle}}**. It's the same for everyone and holds nothing about your home.

## Through Home Assistant's MCP Server {#ha-mcp-server}

Apps that sign in to Home Assistant itself, such as hosted connectors, can reach Phoenix's tools through Home Assistant's MCP Server, at /api/mcp/phoenix_mcp. They use the key bound to [Assist Tool Provider](guide:topic.homeAssistantFeatures#assist-tool-provider) and need an administrator's sign-in.

On that route the key's rate limit doesn't apply, the audit log shows the calls as Assist, and the app gets Phoenix's instructions only if it asks for them.

## When it doesn't connect {#problems}

- **Unauthorized (401)**: the key is wrong, revoked or expired, or was sent in the URL instead of the Authorization header.
- **Forbidden (403)**: a web page tried to connect from another site. Desktop and command-line apps aren't affected.
- **Too many requests (429)**: the key hit its rate limit, or has too many connections open at once. The app should wait and try again.
- **Unavailable (503)**: the kill switch is on, or Phoenix is still starting.

topic.killSwitch.title: What the Kill Switch Stops
topic.killSwitch.body:
The kill switch cuts off every way an AI can reach your home through Phoenix. It doesn't undo actions that already happened.

## What stops {#stops}

- External apps connected over MCP are refused. Requests already running stop at their next check.
- Agent Chat closes, and can't be opened again.
- The Voice Agent only replies that it's unavailable.
- The AI Task entity becomes unavailable.
- Assist Tool Provider offers no tools.
- Approving a waiting request cancels it instead.

## What keeps working {#keeps}

This panel keeps working, so you can review what happened and turn the switch off again. You can still restore a change in Changes and edit MESA profiles, and the in-context profile buttons stay.

## After a restart {#restart}

If the switch is on when Home Assistant starts, Phoenix doesn't open its connections at all. Turning the switch off opens them, without a restart.

Related: [Emergency kill switch](guide:window.settingsSafety#kill-switch)

topic.logRecords.title: What the Logs Record
topic.logRecords.body:
Phoenix keeps two logs. The audit log is a short record of every action and its outcome. The Conversation Log, when it's on, keeps what agents said and did in full.

## What makes an audit entry {#audit-entries}

- **Agent actions**: each tool call from an MCP client, Agent Chat, the voice agent, Assist, AI Task or Home Companion. The entry holds the tool's name and arguments, never its result.
- **Other MCP requests**: listing tools, starting and ending a session, and requests a key wasn't allowed to make.
- **MESA blocks**: an extra entry for each action MESA refused.
- **Approvals**: each request queued for approval, and what happened to it: approved, carried out, rejected, cancelled or failed.
- **Your changes in the panel**: access keys, permissions, settings, MESA profiles, restores, wipes and other administrator actions. These show the administrator instead of an access key. A settings change names what changed, even one that turns logging off.

## What isn't recorded {#not-audited}

Requests without a valid access key, requests while Phoenix is starting or stopped by the kill switch, and chat or voice turns that call no tool. Most panel reads aren't recorded either.

Turn on the [Conversation Log](guide:window.settingsLogs#conversation-log) to see the conversations themselves.

## Outcomes {#outcomes}

- **{{label:audit.outcomeAllowed}}**: carried out.
- **{{label:audit.outcomeDenied}}**: refused by permissions or MESA, or an approval that was rejected, expired or cancelled.
- **{{label:audit.outcomePendingApproval}}**: waiting for your approval.
- **{{label:audit.outcomeRateLimited}}**: the key sent too many requests.
- **{{label:audit.outcomeInvalidRequest}}**, **{{label:audit.outcomeNotFound}}** and **{{label:audit.outcomeNotImplemented}}**: the request was malformed, named something that doesn't exist, or asked for something Phoenix doesn't do.

Which outcomes are recorded is up to the [audit log settings](guide:window.settingsLogs#audit-log).

## How long audit entries are kept {#audit-keeping}

The audit log keeps the newest 10,000 entries by default, and saves them to disk every 15 minutes and when Home Assistant stops. Change both in [{{label:workspace.logsNotifications}}](guide:window.settingsLogs#log-max-entries).

Nothing in the panel clears the audit log on its own. A Phoenix core data wipe does. Removing Phoenix keeps it.

## What the Conversation Log records {#conversation-sources}

- **Agent Chat, the voice agent and AI Task**: each turn, with your words, the reply, and every tool call.
- **MCP clients, Assist and Home Companion**: each tool call and its result. Phoenix doesn't see what the person typed, so there's no prompt.

Work done inside a turn, such as an approved action carried out later, joins that turn. Agent Chat turns in one chat are grouped together.

## What a conversation holds {#conversation-contents}

Each tool call and its full result, changes with their before and after, approvals, errors, and the route a request took. Entries from Agent Chat, voice and AI Task also name the AI provider and model.

Passwords, tokens, keys and alarm or lock codes are hidden before anything is saved. Images and files are noted, not stored. The instructions Phoenix gives the AI aren't recorded, and token usage goes to the routing statistics instead.

## How long conversations are kept {#conversation-keeping}

The newest 100 conversations, for up to 7 days and 25 MB, by default. Change the limits in [{{label:workspace.logsNotifications}}](guide:window.settingsLogs#conversation-log). An entry that's too large keeps its outcome but drops some detail.

Clear the log with **{{label:conversations.clear}}** in the Conversation Log window. A core data wipe clears it too.

## Finding the same request in both logs {#linked}

A tool call's request ID is the same in both logs, and so is an approval's ID. In the audit log, filter by **{{label:audit.rowRequestId}}** or **{{label:audit.rowResource}}**; in the Conversation Log, search for it.

topic.mesaRules.title: How MESA Decides
topic.mesaRules.body:
MESA checks every action an agent takes on a device, after the access key has allowed it. A profile describes how careful to be with what it covers. This page explains how profiles at different levels add up, and what happens when an action breaks one.

## Levels {#levels}

A profile covers one of five things. When an agent acts on an entity, MESA gathers every profile that covers it, most specific first:

- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelEntity}}**: the entity itself.
- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelDevice}}**: the device the entity belongs to, including entities the device gains later.
- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelParentDevice}}**: for a device that's part of a larger one, the larger device's profile. A hub that a device connects through doesn't count.
- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelArea}}**: the entity's area, or else its device's area.
- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelIntegration}}**: the integration that created the entity, such as hue.
- **{{label:mesa.scopeLabelDomain}}**: every entity of one kind, such as every lock.

You add profiles for all of these in **{{label:workspace.profileEditor}}**, except the main device, which is a device profile seen from its parts.

## How profiles combine {#combining}

MESA combines profiles field by field, not profile by profile.

- **Control mode**: the most restrictive mode any level sets wins. A specific profile can't loosen a broader one, so an Autonomous lock entity under a Prohibited lock domain stays Prohibited. The one exception is below.
- **Privacy level**: the most restrictive level wins, in the same way.
- **Triggers automations**: Likely at any level wins. Otherwise the most specific level wins.
- **Everything else**: the most specific level wins, but a value written or confirmed by a person, or written by the device's maker, outranks an inferred one at any level.

The one way to loosen a control mode is an entity override with a written reason, which can turn Confirm into Autonomous but never relaxes Prohibited or Read-Only. Profile Editor can't set it; it only arrives by import.

Related: [Effective Resolution](guide:window.mesaEditor#effective-resolution)

## The built-in baseline {#baseline}

An entity that no profile covers follows a built-in baseline: lights are Autonomous, locks and alarm panels are Prohibited, and everything else is Confirm.

A profile changes that:

- **A profile that sets a control mode replaces the baseline**, at whatever level it sits, even when it's looser. A Confirm profile on a lock makes the lock Confirm instead of Prohibited.
- **A profile that leaves control mode unset keeps the baseline**, but anything Autonomous becomes Confirm. A tags-only profile on a light makes that light need confirmation.

So an Autonomous domain profile for locks makes every lock Autonomous. Check a profile's effect in [Effective Resolution](guide:window.mesaEditor#effective-resolution) before you rely on it.

Deployment defaults can replace the built-in baseline for unprofiled entities. They come from an imported archive; Profile Editor can't edit them.

## What happens when an action breaks a rule {#modes}

What MESA does depends on **{{label:settings.mesaModeLabel}}** in [Settings](guide:window.settingsSafety#mesa-mode), and on the profile's own **{{label:mesa.fieldEnforcement}}**.

- **{{label:settings.mesaModeOff}}**: MESA allows everything.
- **{{label:settings.mesaModeAdvisory}}** (default): Prohibited actions and broken limits only warn the agent, and Confirm actions run without approval. Read-Only entities and privacy denials still block.
- **{{label:settings.mesaModeEnforced}}**: Prohibited and Read-Only actions and broken limits are blocked. Confirm actions wait for your approval in [Approvals](guide:topic.approvalLifecycle).

A profile set to **{{label:mesa.modeEnforced}}** is enforced while the setting is Advisory. While the setting is Off, nothing is enforced.

When an action targets several entities, MESA drops the blocked ones and the action runs on the rest. A warning or a block reaches the agent with the reason.

## Privacy {#privacy}

A **{{label:mesa.privRestricted}}** privacy level makes an Autonomous entity need confirmation. People are always at least **{{label:mesa.privSensitive}}**.

An imported profile can also deny access to certain personas. That denial blocks the action in every mode except Off, including camera images.

## What MESA covers {#coverage}

MESA covers every way an agent changes something: MCP clients, Agent Chat, the voice agent, Assist and AI Task. It applies to pass-through access keys too.

It checks device actions, renaming and removing entities and devices, integration and helper changes, areas and floors, calendar writes and notifications.

Reading a state isn't checked, except camera images. Automations and scripts run inside Home Assistant, so their actions aren't checked again. To control when an agent starts one, give the automation or script its own profile.

## What Profile Editor can't set {#not-in-editor}

A profile can also hold declared limits (such as a maximum temperature), time windows when stricter rules apply, privacy denials for certain personas, and the entity override. These arrive only in an imported archive.

Saving a profile in Profile Editor replaces the whole profile with what the form shows, so it removes these fields.

Related: [{{label:mesa.importTitle}}](guide:window.mesaProfiles#import)

topic.routingStatistics.title: Reading Routing Statistics
topic.routingStatistics.body:
Routing statistics show how often Phoenix carried out a command without your AI model, and what the rest cost. Agent Chat and the Voice Agent are counted separately.

## The headline {#headline}

The percentage at the top is the share of messages handled by sentence matching or the decision provider. The higher it is, the fewer full model turns you paid for.

## The counts {#counts}

Each message is counted once, by its outcome. If a message used your AI model at any point, it counts as sent to it.

- **{{label:routingStats.local}}**: Home Assistant's sentence matching carried it out.
- **{{label:routingStats.decision}}**: the decision provider carried it out.
- **{{label:routingStats.provider}}**: your AI model handled it.
- **{{label:routingStats.pending}}**: waiting for your approval.
- **{{label:routingStats.failed}}** and **{{label:routingStats.cancelled}}**: messages that didn't finish.

A message sent to your AI model can also fail or be cancelled, so the rows don't always add up.

## Tokens {#tokens}

The token rows total what the decision provider and your AI model reported using. Providers don't always report usage. Requests without a report are counted below the totals.

## Refresh and reset {#refresh-and-reset}

**{{label:common.refresh}}** loads the latest counts. **{{label:routingStats.reset}}** sets this window's counts back to zero, after you confirm. Messages still in progress aren't counted after a reset.

Counts are saved every 30 seconds and survive a restart. Deleting core data in [Data Management](guide:window.settingsSafety#wipe-core) clears them.

topic.security.title: Security
topic.security.body:
Phoenix lets AI agents work in your home, so it's built to give each one only what you allow and to keep secrets out of reach. This page explains what Phoenix protects, what it can't, and what you can do to stay safe.

Related: [What every action goes through](guide:topic.about#checks), [What Agents Can Do](guide:topic.tools)

## Access keys {#keys}

Each app connects with its own access key. Phoenix stores only a fingerprint of it, so the key itself is shown once, when you create or rotate it.

- An app must send the key in its Authorization header. A key placed in a web address is refused.
- A browser request from a page outside Home Assistant is refused, so a malicious website can't reach Phoenix through your browser.
- A revoked or expired key stops working straight away. Requests already running stop at their next check.

Related: [Keeping the key safe](guide:topic.connecting#credentials), [{{label:accessKeys.rotate}}](guide:window.accessKeys#rotate), [{{label:accessKeys.revoke}}](guide:window.accessKeys#revoke)

## What agents never see {#hidden}

Phoenix removes some data before an agent sees it, whatever the key allows, pass-through included:

- Phoenix's own entities and the sensors it creates for each key.
- Camera stream and picture addresses, and access tokens.
- Any attribute whose name suggests a secret, such as one containing password, token, secret, key or session.

Entities outside the key's scope look as if they don't exist. In action results and dashboards they show as `<redacted>`.

## What Phoenix can't catch {#gaps}

Removing secrets works by name, so a secret under an ordinary name gets through. Keep passwords and keys in secrets.yaml, which no agent can read.

- YAML configuration returns your files exactly as written. A password typed straight into one is visible to the agent.
- Logs are free text. Phoenix removes access keys, tokens and passwords in web addresses, but other secrets in a log line can slip through.

Give these capabilities only to agents that need them.

Related: [Files and YAML](guide:topic.tools#files), [Configuration, templates and logs](guide:topic.tools#configuration)

## Home data is untrusted {#untrusted}

A device name or a state can contain text written by anyone, such as "ignore your instructions". When Phoenix describes the home to a model, it labels the data as untrusted content, not instructions.

That helps, but no model is perfect. Keep changes you care about on Confirm, so you see each one before it runs.

Related: [{{label:caps.modeConfirm}}](guide:window.capabilities#modes)

## Request limits {#request-limits}

- A request body can be up to 1 MB, and a batch up to 50 requests. Each request in a batch counts toward the rate limit.
- External apps are rate limited per key, by default 60 requests a minute and 10 a second. Agent Chat, Voice, Assist and AI Task aren't.
- A key over its limit is told when to try again.

Related: [{{label:accessKeys.cardRateLimiting}}](guide:window.keySettings#rate-limiting)

## The administrator side {#admin}

The panel and its settings need a Home Assistant administrator. Access keys can't open them. Any administrator credential works, including an administrator's long-lived access token, and it can create keys with any capability.

Keep the number of administrators small, and protect their tokens. Home Assistant's MCP Server reaches Phoenix with an administrator's sign-in and without Phoenix's rate limit. Bind a narrow key to it.

Related: [Through Home Assistant's MCP Server](guide:topic.connecting#ha-mcp-server)

## What's stored where {#stored}

Phoenix keeps its data in Home Assistant's storage folder. Access keys are stored only as fingerprints. AI provider API keys and recorded conversations are kept there as they are, not encrypted.

Home Assistant backups include that folder. Treat backups and the configuration folder as secret.

Related: [What the Logs Record](guide:topic.logRecords)

## Keeping it safe {#checklist}

- Give each app its own key, with only the capabilities it needs.
- Use pass-through only for an agent you fully trust. It also opens Diagnostics and Service response data.
- Keep System log read, Diagnostics and YAML configuration for agents that need them.
- Before setting an expiry on a key used by Voice, AI Task or Assist, know that expiry unlinks it.
- Use HTTPS when apps connect over a network you don't trust. The key travels with every request.

Related: [What Pass-Through Opens](guide:topic.passThrough)

## If something goes wrong {#emergency}

If a key leaks, rotate it. The old value stops working at once, and the app needs the new one. Revoke a key you no longer use.

If an agent misbehaves, turn on the [{{label:settings.killSwitchCard}}](guide:topic.killSwitch). It refuses new agent work and stops running requests at their next check. It can't undo actions already sent, so check [{{label:attention.title}}](guide:window.attention) afterwards.

## Removing Phoenix completely {#removing}

Deleting the integration revokes the keys but keeps settings, logs and archived keys. To remove Phoenix's data too, use **{{label:settings.wipeCoreLabel}}** first.

Related: [Removing Phoenix MCP](guide:topic.install#removing), [{{label:settings.wipeCoreLabel}}](guide:window.settingsSafety#wipe-core)

topic.tools.title: What Agents Can Do
topic.tools.body:
An agent works through tools. This page explains them by group: what they let an agent do, which capabilities allow them, and the limits worth knowing. Clients read each tool's details from the tool itself.

Two settings decide every action. [{{label:accessKeys.cardCapabilities}}](guide:window.capabilities) decide what kind of thing an agent may do. The [{{label:accessKeys.permissionsTree}}](guide:window.permissions) decides which entities it may do it to.

## How capabilities apply {#rules}

- A tool whose capability is Deny isn't offered to the agent, and a call to it is refused before it runs.
- **{{label:accessKeys.announceAllLabel}}** lists every tool anyway, for troubleshooting. The agent still can't use the hidden ones.
- Confirm holds a change for your approval. Reads that use the same capability run straight away.
- A result that lists many entities stops at about 64 KB.

Pass-through allows most read capabilities without setting them. Every capability that changes something keeps its own setting.

Related: [Deny, Allow and Confirm](guide:window.capabilities#modes), [What pass-through opens](guide:topic.passThrough)

## Reading the home {#reading}

Agents read current states, history, statistics, calendars, to-do lists and a summary of the whole home. They see only the entities the tree lets them read. Sensitive attributes are always removed.

Most reads need no capability; the tree alone decides. Camera stills need one, and so does picking history or statistics entities with a search filter.

- History and statistics come in pages of up to 1000 rows.
- A calendar read covers up to 31 days and 500 events.
- Camera images are at most 2048 pixels on a side.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_camera_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#camera-read), [{{label:caps.cap_search.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#search)

## Controlling devices {#controlling}

Agents turn things on and off, set lights, fans, climate, covers and volume, control media and vacuums, and cancel timers. These are the same commands Home Assistant's own assistant uses. Every target needs Write in the tree.

Locks, alarms, covers and valves also need Physical control. On Confirm, a command that includes one waits for your approval. On Deny, the agent can't control them.

Announcing a message through Assist satellites needs Broadcast. MESA checks every command last, after the capability and the tree.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_physical_control.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#physical-control), [{{label:caps.cap_broadcast.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#broadcast)

Related: [How MESA decides](guide:topic.mesaRules)

## Running any action {#actions}

Agents can also run any Home Assistant action on targets they can write, and preview the result first. A few actions need more:

- Restarting or stopping Home Assistant needs Restart.
- Reloading automations, scripts, scenes, helpers or the core configuration needs YAML configuration.
- An action's returned data needs Service response data. Without it, the action still runs.
- ESPHome device actions need only Write on the device. MESA doesn't check them, and doesn't check reloads or restarts either.

Other actions without a target are refused. So are calendar changes, which have their own tools. An action still running after 30 seconds is reported as possibly incomplete.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_restart.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#restart), [{{label:caps.cap_yaml_edit.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#yaml-edit), [{{label:caps.cap_service_response.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#service-response), [{{label:caps.cap_search.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#search) for previews

## Lists and calendars {#lists}

Agents add, change and remove to-do items, which needs only Write on the list. They create, change and delete calendar events, which also needs Calendar write. MESA checks both. Each calendar change leaves a receipt the agent can check later.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_calendar_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#calendar-write)

## Waiting for a change {#waiting}

An agent can wait up to 30 seconds for an entity to change or reach a state, to confirm that an action worked. The tree and authority are checked again when the wait ends.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_config_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#config-read)

## Home Companion {#home-companion}

A [{{label:personas.home_companion.label}}](guide:window.persona#home-companion) key offers a single tool. The app sends one plain request, such as "turn off the downstairs lights". Phoenix carries it out with its own model, checks the result and reports back.

- It controls lights, fans, switches, climate, covers, valves, media players, vacuums, humidifiers and timers.
- It reads sensors, weather, calendars and the sun, but can't change them. Sensors are limited to temperature, humidity, light, power, energy and battery.
- Locks, alarms and cameras are out of its reach.
- Each key handles one request at a time, with up to 8 actions and 2 minutes per request.
- Pass-through and **{{label:accessKeys.announceAllLabel}}** are always off.

In Agent Chat it uses the chat's model. Everywhere else it uses the Voice Agent's provider and model.

Related: [Voice Agent](guide:topic.homeAssistantFeatures#voice-agent)

## Automations and scripts {#automations}

Agents read, create, edit and delete the automations and scripts that Home Assistant's own editor manages. On Confirm, the approval shows the new configuration, or the before and after of an edit. Every change is kept in [{{label:shell.tabChanges}}](guide:topic.configurationHistory).

An automation runs as Home Assistant, not as the agent. Its actions aren't limited by the key's tree or by MESA. So these capabilities let an agent control devices indirectly. Use Confirm to review each one.

- Only the editor's own files change. Automations and scripts written by hand elsewhere in YAML are refused.
- Listing them needs Registry read, and shows only those whose entity the key can read.
- Blueprints need Manage blueprints plus the capability for the blueprint's kind, automation or script.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_automation_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#automation-write), [{{label:caps.cap_script_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#script-write), [{{label:caps.cap_blueprint_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#blueprint-write)

## Scenes {#scenes}

Agents read, create, edit and delete scenes in Home Assistant's scene editor. Every entity in a scene needs Write in the tree, even just to read the scene. MESA doesn't check scene changes.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_scene_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#scene-write)

## Helpers {#helpers}

Agents create, edit and delete helpers: toggles, numbers, text, lists, dates, buttons, counters, timers, schedules, zones, tags and people. They also manage helpers set up through an integration, such as Template, and change their settings.

- MESA checks helper changes. A MESA Confirm asks for its own approval, even when Manage helpers is Allow.
- Only zones, tags and people follow the tree. Other helpers are limited by the capability and MESA alone.
- Deleting a Template helper also needs Integration management.
- Helpers defined in YAML can't be changed.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_helper_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#helper-write), [{{label:caps.cap_integration_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#integration-write)

## Dashboards {#dashboards}

Agents list, create, edit and delete dashboards, read and search their layouts, change cards and list the installed custom cards. All of it needs Manage dashboards, reads included.

- The tree and MESA don't limit dashboard changes. Entities the key can't read show as `<redacted>`, and a change that still contains one is refused.
- A layout that wouldn't display is refused.
- Deleting a dashboard saves its layout first, so it can be restored.
- The custom card list comes from a browser that opened the panel, refreshed at most every 10 minutes.

Resources, the JavaScript and CSS that every dashboard loads, need Dashboard resources.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_lovelace_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#lovelace-write), [{{label:caps.cap_dashboard_resources.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#dashboard-resources)

## Restoring a change {#restore}

An agent can put back one of its own earlier changes to a Template helper, blueprint, Energy setup, dashboard or dashboard resource. It asks for a receipt first, then sends the restore, which goes through the usual approval for that capability. An agent sees only its own records.

Allowed by: any of [{{label:caps.cap_helper_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#helper-write), [{{label:caps.cap_blueprint_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#blueprint-write), [{{label:caps.cap_energy_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#energy-write), [{{label:caps.cap_lovelace_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#lovelace-write), [{{label:caps.cap_dashboard_resources.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#dashboard-resources)

Related: [What a restore can put back](guide:topic.configurationHistory#restore)

## MESA profiles {#mesa}

Agents read the MESA profiles of entities they can read, and see why a profile resolved the way it did. They can also take a short lease, up to 30 seconds, on entities they can write. A lease tells others the agent is working there; it grants nothing.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_config_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#config-read)

Related: [How MESA decides](guide:topic.mesaRules)

## Configuration, templates and logs {#configuration}

- Configuration read covers Home Assistant's basic setup, the Energy setup, solar forecasts and blueprints.
- Manage Energy dashboard changes one part of the Energy setup.
- Template render renders templates in a separate, limited process. It works on a copy of the states the key can read, for up to 5 seconds.
- System log read covers warnings and errors, the logbook and notifications.
- Integration log levels changes how much an integration logs, such as turning on debug logging. A change can end after 5 to 120 minutes, last until the next restart, or stay until cleared.

Template functions that need Home Assistant itself, such as area or device lookups, return nothing.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_config_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#config-read), [{{label:caps.cap_energy_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#energy-write), [{{label:caps.cap_template_render.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#template-render), [{{label:caps.cap_log_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#log-read), [{{label:caps.cap_log_control.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#log-control)

## Discovery and diagnostics {#diagnostics}

These tools only read. They help an agent find its way before it acts.

- Search & discovery searches and describes entities, areas and how things relate, compares them, and finds what actions are available.
- Registry read lists areas, floors, zones, devices, labels, automations, scripts, scenes and helpers.
- Automation traces reads how automations ran.
- Diagnostics checks the configuration and reads system health, repairs, radio networks and the ESPHome overview.

A configuration check names the file and line only when YAML configuration isn't Deny.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_search.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#search), [{{label:caps.cap_registry_read.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#registry-read), [{{label:caps.cap_traces.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#traces), [{{label:caps.cap_diagnostics.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#diagnostics)

## Files and YAML {#files}

Read files lets an agent read text files in the www, themes and custom_templates folders, up to 1 MiB each. It can't write them.

YAML configuration lets an agent read your YAML files, apart from secrets.yaml, the esphome folder and hidden files. Files come back exactly as written, so a password typed straight into one is visible. No tool writes YAML configuration.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_filesystem.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#filesystem), [{{label:caps.cap_yaml_edit.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#yaml-edit)

## ESPHome {#esphome}

Agents read and search ESPHome device configuration, with passwords and keys masked. With the ESPHome Device Builder add-on, they can also validate, compile, read device logs, analyse memory and check connections. Without the add-on, only reading and searching remain.

Compiling, cleaning and memory analysis need Write on the device. Installing firmware needs ESPHome firmware flashing and Write on the device.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_esphome_yaml.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#esphome-yaml), [{{label:caps.cap_esphome_flash.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#esphome-flash)

## Integrations, devices and the system {#system}

- Integration management adds, enables, disables, reloads and removes integrations, and removes devices.
- Integration reconfiguration changes an integration's settings.
- Manage entity registry renames entities and devices and changes entity IDs, areas, floors, labels and categories.
- Radio management changes Zigbee networks. Groups, bindings and device properties also need Physical control.
- Backup creates and lists backups, but can't restore one.
- Restart or stop Home Assistant restarts it. The agent is told not to retry by itself.
- Notifications sends a notification.

A backup waits up to 45 seconds and never goes to Home Assistant Cloud. Without a backup encryption key it isn't encrypted, and it includes secrets.yaml.

Allowed by: [{{label:caps.cap_integration_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#integration-write), [{{label:caps.cap_integration_reconfigure.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#integration-reconfigure), [{{label:caps.cap_registry_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#registry-write), [{{label:caps.cap_radio_write.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#radio-write), [{{label:caps.cap_backup.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#backup), [{{label:caps.cap_restart.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#restart), [{{label:caps.cap_notify.label}}](guide:window.capabilities#notify)

## The key's own state {#introspection}

Every key can check its own approval requests, wait up to 30 seconds for up to 50 of them, and read its capability summary and audit entries. These need no capability. Requests from another key look like they don't exist.

## On Voice, Assist and AI Task {#household}

Anyone in the household can speak to Assist or the Voice Agent. For someone who isn't a Home Assistant administrator, the key keeps five capabilities at most. They are Search & discovery, Registry read, Physical control, Broadcast and Service response data. The rest count as Deny.

The approval and audit tools are hidden too, and Home Assistant's admin-only actions are refused. A speaker Home Assistant can't identify is treated the same way. AI Task always runs like this.

Related: [Voice Agent, AI Task or Assist Tool Provider](guide:topic.homeAssistantFeatures), [Assist and the Voice Agent](guide:topic.permissionResolution#household)

topic.windows.title: Working with Windows
topic.windows.body:
Each workspace is a set of windows you can arrange as you like. Phoenix remembers the arrangement for you, on every computer you sign in from.

## The toolbar {#toolbar}

The buttons switch workspaces. Approvals shows how many requests are waiting. **{{label:shell.agentChat}}** opens Agent Chat, and **{{label:shell.documentation}}** turns the Help Bar and the Guide on or off.

The second row holds the tools of the windows you have open, such as Filters or Refresh. A tool several windows share shows once and acts on all of them.

## {{label:workspace.toolbarOptions}} {#toolbar-options}

Open them from the toolbar's last button, or right-click the toolbar.

- **{{label:workspace.iconsOnly}}** (default) or **{{label:workspace.iconsAndText}}**.
- **{{label:workspace.singleRow}}** puts the tools on the same row as the workspace buttons while they fit, and goes back to two rows when they don't.
- Dock the toolbar along any edge, or **{{label:workspace.floatToolbar}}** to place it anywhere. You can also drag its grip to float it.
- **{{label:workspace.collapseToolbar}}** shrinks it to its grip.

## The title bar {#title-bar}

Drag a window by its title bar. The buttons beside the title fold it to its title bar, float it above the workspace, maximize it, and close it.

A floating window stays put while the workspace scrolls. **{{label:workspace.dockWindow}}** puts it back where it was. From its menu, the Move items nudge it across the workspace, and **{{label:workspace.resizeKeyboard}}** sizes it.

## The window menu {#window-menu}

Open it from the title bar's menu button, or right-click the title bar.

- **{{label:workspace.moveLeft}}** and the other moves put the window past its neighbor on that side, without dragging.
- **{{label:workspace.resizeKeyboard}}**: Left and Right Arrow change the width, Up and Down the height. Press Escape when you're done.
- **{{label:workspace.pinTop}}** and **{{label:workspace.pinBottom}}** keep a window in a band that doesn't scroll. **{{label:workspace.unpin}}** returns it.
- **{{label:workspace.addToMy}}** copies it to [My Workspace](guide:workspace.my).
- **{{label:workspace.alwaysLabels}}** shows its tools with their names, even when the toolbar shows icons only.

## The Guide {#guide}

The Guide is one window over every workspace. It shows the page for the window you're working in, and selecting a control takes it to the section about that control. Use Back and Forward, Contents and Search at the top to find your way.

Fold, maximize and close it from its title bar, or move and resize it with the keyboard from its menu. Closing it anywhere closes it everywhere.

**{{label:agentchat.popOut}}** moves the Guide to a browser window of its own, so it can sit beside Home Assistant. It keeps following what you select in the panel. **{{label:agentchat.popIn}}** brings it back, and closing that window closes the Guide.

It stays popped out only while the Phoenix panel is open. After a reload it's back inside the panel. It isn't offered on a phone, or while it sits beside the setup.

## Arranging windows {#arranging}

Drop a window on another window's edge to put it beside, above or below it. Up to four windows fit side by side. Drag the border between two windows to resize them.

Access Keys and Settings scroll, and each window is as tall as its content. The other workspaces fit the screen, so their windows share its height.

## Closing and showing windows {#closing}

Closing a window hides it in this workspace. Show it again from **{{label:workspace.options}}**, and it returns to the place it had.

Help comes back from **{{label:help.showHelpBar}}** in the Documentation menu, and Needs Attention from **{{label:workspace.showAttention}}**. In My Workspace, closing a window removes it.

## Your arrangements {#defaults}

**{{label:workspace.options}}** also opens by right-clicking an empty part of the workspace.

- **{{label:workspace.saveMyDefault}}** keeps this workspace's arrangement, including table columns. **{{label:workspace.restoreMyDefault}}** brings it back.
- **{{label:workspace.restoreOriginal}}** puts this workspace back as Phoenix first arranged it, and resets its table columns. Your My Default stays.
- **{{label:workspace.restorePanelDefaults}}** does that for every workspace, and also resets the toolbar, Help and the Guide, and empties My Workspace. Every My Default stays.

## How arrangements are saved {#saved}

Your arrangement is saved as you work, for your Home Assistant user. Another computer picks it up the next time it loads Phoenix. Phones keep an arrangement of their own.

## On a phone {#phones}

Windows stack in one column you scroll, with the toolbar at the top. Fold a window from its title bar. Window menus, dragging and Workspace Options are desktop only.

## Keyboard {#keyboard}

F6 moves to the next area: the toolbar, each window in the order you see them, the Guide and Agent Chat. Shift+F6 moves back. Coming back to an area returns you to where you were in it, and Tab still moves between the controls inside it.

Every menu opens with Enter, Space or Down Arrow. Use the arrow keys, Home and End to move through it, and Escape to close it. The keyboard's menu key opens the menu of the control in focus.

window.agentChat.title: {{label:agentchat.title}}
window.agentChat.body:
Talk to an AI agent about your home. It acts through one of your access keys, so it can do only what that key allows, and every action is checked and logged like any other.

Related: [{{label:settings.agentcliCard}} settings](guide:window.settingsChat), [{{label:workspace.aiProviders}}](guide:window.settingsProviders)

## Opening Agent Chat {#opening}

Select **{{label:shell.agentChat}}** on the toolbar. It appears once you have an access key and an AI provider account. Shift+A also opens and closes it, unless you're typing in a field. It needs keyboard shortcuts turned on in your Home Assistant profile.

With **{{label:settings.agentcliGlobalLabel}}** on (the default), Chat stays open as you move around Home Assistant. With it off, Chat lives in the Phoenix panel, and leaving the panel ends a reply in progress.

While the kill switch is on, Chat closes and can't be opened.

## The window {#window}

Drag it by its title bar and resize it from any edge. Edges near the side of the screen snap to it. Minimize shrinks it to a small bar you can move, and Maximize fills the screen.

**{{label:agentchat.popOut}}** moves Chat to a browser window of its own, and the conversation carries on there. On a phone, Chat opens full screen.

On a computer, you can also dock Chat in [My Workspace](guide:workspace.my#chat). Closing Chat doesn't clear the conversation.

## {{label:agentchat.options}} {#options}

The menu button in the title bar:

- **{{label:agentchat.connection}}** shows the connection fields below.
- **{{label:agentchat.verbose}}** shows each tool the agent calls, its result, and the model's reasoning when it shares it. Off by default.
- **{{label:agentchat.showTimestamps}}** adds the time under each message. Off by default.
- **{{label:agentchat.showFooter}}** shows the footer with text size and token use. On by default.
- **{{label:agentchat.decreaseTextSize}}** and **{{label:agentchat.increaseTextSize}}** change the size of the conversation's text.

These choices are kept in this browser.

## {{label:agentchat.connection}} {#connection}

The line under the title shows the access key, provider and model in use. Select its triangle to change them.

- **{{label:agentchat.accessKey}}**: the agent works with this key's permissions.
- **{{label:agentchat.provider}}**: the AI provider account that runs the agent.
- **{{label:agentchat.model}}**: the model to use, from that account's list.
- **{{label:agentchat.thinking}}** and **{{label:agentchat.temperature}}**: shown only when the model offers them. Leave Temperature empty for the provider's default.

Changing the access key or provider starts a new conversation. You can't change the key, provider or model while a reply is running.

## Talking to the agent {#conversation}

Press Enter to send, or Shift+Enter for a new line. While the agent works, a line shows what it's doing and how long it has waited for the provider. **{{label:agentchat.stop}}** ends the reply and puts your message back in the box.

Copy a message with its copy button. The footer shows the tokens used in this conversation, and how much of the model's context the last request took.

## Pausing to check in {#check-in}

After a number of steps without your input, the agent pauses and asks whether to continue. A step is one request to the model plus the tools it asked for. Select **{{label:agentchat.continue}}** to let it go on.

Approving or rejecting an action resets the count. Set the number in [{{label:settings.agentcliStepsLabel}}](guide:window.settingsChat#chat-steps).

## Images {#images}

Paste an image, drop it on the window, or use the attach button: up to 4 per message. Phoenix shrinks large photos before sending them.

Images can't be sent with a Home Companion key, or to a model that only reads text. They aren't kept after a reload, so the agent can't see them again later.

## Approvals in the chat {#approvals}

When an action needs your approval, a card appears in the conversation. Select **{{label:agentchat.approve}}** or **{{label:agentchat.reject}}**, or **{{label:agentchat.review}}** to see the full change first in Approvals.

The agent waits up to 15 minutes. Approving in Approvals or from a notification updates the card too. Stopping, closing Chat or reloading cancels actions that are still waiting.

Related: [How an approval works](guide:topic.approvalLifecycle)

## {{label:agentchat.clearHistory}} {#clear}

Starts a new conversation straight away, without asking. Typing /clear does the same. The Conversation Log keeps what it already recorded.

## What's kept, and where {#privacy}

The conversation is kept in this browser for your Home Assistant user, so it's still there after a reload. The newest messages, within [{{label:settings.agentcliScrollbackLabel}}](guide:window.settingsChat#chat-memory), are sent to the provider with each message. Phoenix keeps no copy on the server, except in the Conversation Log when that's on.

Only administrators can use Agent Chat.

window.archivedAccessKeys.body:
Keys you revoked and keys that expired. **{{label:accessKeys.showArchived}}** on the toolbar opens this window over the workspace. Selecting a key in the list closes it again.

An archived key keeps its name, dates and who created it. Its capabilities, permissions and settings are gone, and it can never be used again.

window.auditLog.title: {{label:shell.tabAudit}}
window.auditLog.body:
Each action agents and administrators took through Phoenix, newest first.

Related: [What the Logs Record](guide:topic.logRecords)

## The list {#list}

Choose an entry to read it in [{{label:workspace.logDetails}}](guide:window.logDetails). Up and Down Arrow move through the list.

- **{{label:audit.rowAccess}}** says whether the key used its permissions or [pass-through](guide:topic.passThrough).
- **{{label:audit.rowMesa}}** shows {{label:mesa.modeAdvisory}} when MESA warned the agent but let the action run.
- **{{label:audit.rowIp}}** is the caller's IP address, or the Phoenix feature that made the call, such as Agent Chat.
- **{{label:audit.colAccessKey}}** shows the key's current name, even if it was renamed since.

The log loads 100 entries at a time; select **{{label:common.loadMore}}** for more. Sorting by anything other than newest first sorts only the entries loaded so far.

Sort, move and hide columns from the column header's menu, and drag a header's edge to resize one.

## {{label:logs.filters}} {#filters}

Narrow the list by **{{label:audit.rowOutcome}}**, **{{label:audit.colAccessKey}}** and time, and by text in **{{label:audit.rowMethod}}**, **{{label:audit.rowResource}}** and **{{label:audit.rowIp}}**. **{{label:audit.rowRequestId}}** finds one exact request, such as one from the Conversation Log. A time window such as the past 5 minutes moves on as the log updates.

Hiding the filters stops them applying until you show them again. When both logs are open, one **{{label:logs.filters}}** button shows the filters of both.

## Live updates {#updates}

New entries appear every 5 seconds while the window is shown and unfolded. **{{label:logs.pauseUpdates}}** holds the list still while you read it. While paused, **{{label:common.refresh}}** loads the newest entries once.

## From Needs Attention {#attention}

**{{label:attention.showInAudit}}** in the Needs Attention window opens this log filtered to that one request.

window.chatRoutingStatistics.title: {{label:routingStats.chatWindow}}
window.chatRoutingStatistics.body:
Counts how Agent Chat's messages were handled since the last reset: by Home Assistant's sentence matching, the decision provider, or your AI model. Open it with **{{label:routingStats.show}}** in the {{label:settings.agentcliCard}} window, or from **{{label:workspace.options}}**.

Every Agent Chat message counts, even with **{{label:routing.enableChat}}** off. AI Task and external apps aren't counted.

Related: [Reading the statistics](guide:topic.routingStatistics), [Handle chat commands directly](guide:window.settingsChat#chat-commands)

window.help.title: {{label:help.title}}
window.help.body:
A short line about the control under the pointer, or the one in focus when the pointer is elsewhere. It sits along the bottom of every workspace and doesn't scroll.

Pointing at the Help window itself keeps its text, so you can read it. For more than a line, open the Guide from the Documentation menu.

## Showing and hiding Help {#showing}

**{{label:help.showHelpBar}}** in the Documentation menu shows or hides Help in every workspace. It's on by default.

Closing Help in one workspace hides it there only. Show it again from **{{label:help.showHelpBar}}**, which then applies to every workspace again.

Help isn't available on a phone.

window.itemHistory.title: {{label:workspace.itemHistory}}
window.itemHistory.body:
Every recorded change to the chosen item, newest first, with the chosen one marked. Choose a change to compare it, and **{{label:workspace.previousRecord}}** and **{{label:workspace.nextRecord}}** then move through this list.

It opens by itself, under the Changes list, when the item has more than one change. If you close it, it stays closed; reopen it from **{{label:workspace.options}}**.

Phoenix keeps the 20 newest changes to each item. When an entity is renamed, its changes move to its new ID, so its history stays in one list.

window.mesaEditor.title: {{label:workspace.profileEditor}}
window.mesaEditor.body:
The profile you chose in [{{label:workspace.mesaProfiles}}](guide:window.mesaProfiles), or a new one. The title says what kind of profile it is and what it covers.

## What it covers {#target}

For a new profile, choose what it covers from the list. Targets that already have a profile of this kind aren't offered. Once a profile is saved, its target can't change.

## {{label:mesa.semanticTags}} {#tags}

Standard MESA tags that tell agents what the device is and does, such as a door lock or a heater. Tags don't change what agents may do. Add up to 6. **{{label:mesa.showSuggestions}}** lists tags that suit the domain.

## {{label:mesa.fieldControlMode}} {#control-mode}

How agents may change what the profile covers:

- **{{label:mesa.modeAutonomous}}**: agents act freely.
- **{{label:mesa.modeConfirm}}**: actions wait for your approval while MESA is enforced.
- **{{label:mesa.modeReadOnly}}**: agents can't change it, in any MESA mode except Off.
- **{{label:mesa.modeProhibited}}**: agents can't act on it while MESA is enforced. In {{label:settings.mesaModeAdvisory}} mode it only warns them.
- **{{label:mesa.unset}}**: the profile doesn't decide. Other profiles or the built-in baseline do, and the list shows **{{label:mesa.modeInherited}}**.

A new entity profile starts at the mode the entity has now. Other new profiles start at {{label:mesa.unset}}.

Setting a mode replaces the built-in baseline, even when it's looser. A Confirm lock domain profile makes every lock Confirm instead of Prohibited.

Related: [How profiles combine](guide:topic.mesaRules#combining), [The built-in baseline](guide:topic.mesaRules#baseline)

## {{label:mesa.fieldEnforcement}} {#enforcement}

**{{label:mesa.modeEnforced}}** enforces this profile while **{{label:settings.mesaModeLabel}}** in Settings is {{label:settings.mesaModeAdvisory}}. Use it for one device you want strict without making MESA strict everywhere. While the setting is Off, nothing is enforced.

**{{label:mesa.modeAdvisory}}** (default) leaves it to the setting. It isn't saved, so a broader profile that's Enforced still applies.

Related: [What happens when an action breaks a rule](guide:topic.mesaRules#modes)

## {{label:mesa.fieldTriggersAutomations}} {#triggers-automations}

Whether changing this is likely to start automations. MESA checks your automations against it: one marked **{{label:mesa.trigNone}}** that an automation still uses shows a finding in [{{label:workspace.advisory}}](guide:window.mesaAdvisory#validation). Default: **{{label:mesa.trigUnknown}}**.

## Describing the effect {#effect}

**{{label:mesa.fieldReversible}}**, **{{label:mesa.fieldReversibilityCost}}** and **{{label:mesa.fieldSideEffectScope}}** tell agents whether a change can be undone, what undoing it costs, and how far its effect reaches. They inform agents but don't block anything. Each is {{label:mesa.unset}} by default.

## {{label:mesa.fieldPrivacyLevel}} {#privacy-level}

How sensitive the data is that this exposes to agents. Default: **{{label:mesa.privNormal}}**. **{{label:mesa.privRestricted}}** makes an Autonomous profile need confirmation.

Related: [Privacy](guide:topic.mesaRules#privacy)

## Saving {#save}

**{{label:mesa.save}}** stores the profile. It takes effect straight away. For an existing profile, Save is available once you've changed something.

**{{label:mesa.discardChanges}}** puts the form back as it was saved, or closes a new profile. Choosing another profile in the list also replaces the form, so unsaved changes are lost.

Saving replaces the whole profile with what the form shows. Fields the form doesn't show, such as declared limits or time windows from an import, are removed. A vendor profile becomes your own.

Related: [What Profile Editor can't set](guide:topic.mesaRules#not-in-editor)

### Trigger warnings {#save-warnings}

After you save an entity profile, Phoenix checks your automations against it. If it finds a problem, the profile is saved and the warnings are listed under the form. Select **{{label:mesa.dismiss}}** to close them.

### {{label:mesa.delete}} {#delete}

Removes the profile after you confirm in place. What it covered then follows its other profiles, or the built-in baseline.

## {{label:mesa.effectiveResolution}} {#effective-resolution}

For a saved entity profile, the values MESA actually uses once every level is combined. **{{label:mesa.colFrom}}** names the level each value comes from. **{{label:mesa.colOrigin}}** says who wrote it: user for you, developer for an integration's vendor profile.

**{{label:mesa.resolutionWarnings}}** above it means a rule didn't take effect as written, such as an override that MESA ignored. The warnings come from MESA itself and are in English.

## From Home Assistant's pages {#from-home-assistant}

With profile buttons turned on, the same editor opens as a dialog from Home Assistant's own pages, for the entity, device, area or integration you're looking at. Cancel asks before it discards your changes.

Related: [{{label:settings.injectLabel}}](guide:window.settingsGeneral#inject)

window.mesaProfiles.title: {{label:workspace.mesaProfiles}}
window.mesaProfiles.body:
Every MESA profile, whatever it covers, in one list. The list updates every 30 seconds while it's shown.

## {{label:mesa.addProfile}} {#add}

Starts a new profile in [{{label:workspace.profileEditor}}](guide:window.mesaEditor). Choose what it covers: an entity, a device, an area, an integration or a domain. Nothing is saved until you select **{{label:mesa.save}}** there.

Related: [Levels](guide:topic.mesaRules#levels)

## {{label:logs.filters}} {#filters}

Narrows the list by **{{label:mesa.colAppliesTo}}**, **{{label:mesa.colControl}}** and **{{label:mesa.fieldEnforcement}}**. Each choice shows how many profiles it matches. **{{label:mesa.modeInherited}}** means the profile leaves control mode unset.

Search matches the ID, name, type and tags, and keeps working while the filters are hidden. Hiding the filters stops them applying until you show them again. Changing a filter closes the open profile.

## The list {#list}

Choose a profile to open it in [{{label:workspace.profileEditor}}](guide:window.mesaEditor). The control mode shows "{{label:mesa.modeEnforced}}" beside it when the profile is enforced.

**{{label:mesa.colTags}}** and **{{label:mesa.colSource}}** are hidden at first; show them from a column's menu. **{{label:mesa.colSource}}** says **{{label:mesa.vendorBadge}}** for a profile an integration supplies with its code.

## {{label:mesa.delete}} {#delete}

Removes a profile. Select **{{label:mesa.delete}}**, then **{{label:common.confirm}}**, or click anywhere else to back out. What it covered then follows its other profiles, or the built-in baseline if none is left.

An integration's own vendor profile comes back the next time Home Assistant starts, unless you've saved your own profile for that integration.

## MESA Actions {#actions}

The menu holds:

- **{{label:mesa.importTitle}}** and **{{label:mesa.exportTitle}}**, below.
- **{{label:mesa.suggestTitle}}**, which shows or hides that window.
- **{{label:mesa.rescan}}**, which looks for new [suggestions](guide:window.mesaSuggestions) and Advisory findings straight away.
- **{{label:mesa.restoreDismissed}}**, which brings back every suggestion you dismissed.
- **{{label:mesa.restoreNotices}}**, which brings back the findings you dismissed in [{{label:workspace.advisory}}](guide:window.mesaAdvisory).

## {{label:mesa.importTitle}} {#import}

Adds profiles from a MESA archive file, such as one you exported. Select **{{label:mesa.browse}}** and choose the file. Phoenix shows what the archive contains before you import.

Profiles that already exist here are left as they are. Turn on **{{label:mesa.replaceExisting}}** to overwrite them instead; the button turns red and reads **{{label:mesa.importAndReplace}}**. There's no further confirmation.

Imported profiles take effect straight away. Phoenix checks each one and lists any it refused. A profile for a target this home doesn't have shows up in [{{label:workspace.advisory}}](guide:window.mesaAdvisory#orphans).

An archive can hold fields Profile Editor can't set, such as declared limits and time windows, and deployment defaults.

Related: [What Profile Editor can't set](guide:topic.mesaRules#not-in-editor)

## {{label:mesa.exportTitle}} {#export}

Downloads every profile as one archive file, with deployment defaults if you have any. Select **{{label:mesa.export}}** to confirm. The file holds your whole agent safety policy, so keep it somewhere safe.

window.mesaSuggestions.title: {{label:mesa.suggestTitle}}
window.mesaSuggestions.body:
Devices and automations that may need a MESA profile. Phoenix never applies a suggestion itself. Point at a row to read why it's suggested in Help.

## Why something is suggested {#why}

**{{label:mesa.signalUnprotected}}**: a risky device that no profile covers at any level. Locks and alarm panels are suggested as {{label:mesa.modeProhibited}}. Garage doors, doors and gates, valves, sirens, water heaters and firmware updates are suggested as {{label:mesa.modeConfirm}}.

When 5 or more of one kind are uncovered, they become one domain suggestion instead, except garage doors, doors and gates.

**{{label:mesa.signalBlastRadius}}**: an automation, script or scene with no profile that uses a risky device or 8 or more entities. It's suggested as {{label:mesa.modeConfirm}}, so an agent asks before starting it.

Targets written as templates can't be seen, so they're never suggested.

## Acting on a suggestion {#review}

Choose a row to open it in [{{label:workspace.profileEditor}}](guide:window.mesaEditor) as a new profile, filled in with the suggested mode. Check it, change it if you like, and select **{{label:mesa.save}}**. Once saved, the suggestion goes away.

## {{label:mesa.dismiss}} {#dismiss}

Hides a suggestion you don't want, for everyone using this home. Select **{{label:mesa.dismiss}}**, then **{{label:common.confirm}}**.

To see dismissed suggestions again, choose **{{label:mesa.restoreDismissed}}** in the MESA Actions menu. **{{label:mesa.rescan}}**, in the same menu, looks for new suggestions straight away; otherwise the list updates every 30 seconds.

window.notifications.title: {{label:notifications.title}}
window.notifications.body:
The messages Phoenix showed you during this visit to the panel.

## Messages {#toasts}

When something you did in the panel finishes, such as saving a MESA profile, a short message appears at the bottom of the screen for a few seconds. Point at it or move focus into it to keep it there. **{{label:notifications.dismiss}}** hides it.

Problems aren't shown this way. They appear in the window where they happened.

## {{label:notifications.title}} window {#history}

Lists the last 30 messages, newest first, with the time each appeared, and the date for one from an earlier day. They're kept until you reload the panel. **{{label:notifications.clear}}** removes one.

The window starts closed. Open it from **{{label:notifications.showHistory}}** in Workspace Options. It isn't available on a phone, where messages still appear.

window.permissionSummary.title: {{label:accessKeys.permissionSummary}}
window.permissionSummary.body:
Lists every rule set in this key's [{{label:accessKeys.permissionsTree}}](guide:window.permissions): each domain, device or entity set to R, W or D. Rows left at N aren't listed, and neither is what they inherit.

## The table {#summary-table}

Shows each rule's type, name, ID and state. The state reads Deny when a D on the device or domain overrides the rule. Use the column header's menu to sort, move or hide columns, and drag a header's edge to resize one.

Select a row to show it in the {{label:accessKeys.permissionsTree}}. The MESA button on an entity row opens its MESA profile.

## An empty summary {#empty}

An empty summary means nothing is granted in the tree. Tools that don't use the tree, such as reading configuration or managing automations, still work if the key's capabilities allow them.

On a pass-through key, the summary says the key skips the tree instead.

window.permissions.title: {{label:accessKeys.permissionsTree}}
window.permissions.body:
Decides which devices and entities the key can reach, and whether it can only read them or also control them. A new key reaches nothing until you grant something here.

## Setting access {#states}

Each row has four buttons:

- **N**: no setting of its own. The row follows the level above it.
- **R**: read only.
- **W**: read and control.
- **D**: deny. It overrides every grant above and below it.

Each change saves straight away. Click the active button again to go back to N, or drag across rows to set many at once.

The word after each name shows the result: WRITE, READ, DENY, NO ACCESS or NOT FOUND.

Related: [How a permission is decided](guide:topic.permissionResolution)

## The tree {#tree}

Domains are at the top, with their devices and entities below. Entities without a device are grouped under **{{label:perms.deviceless}}**, and a device made of parts shows them nested beneath it.

A grant on a domain or device also covers entities added to it later; the **{{label:perms.dynamicBadge}}** badge says so. A "!" marks domains where W reaches further than it looks, such as homeassistant, backup, automation, script and scene.

A row marked Missing is a grant on an entity that isn't in Home Assistant's list of enabled entities any more. Unmatched Device Permissions, at the end, lists grants on devices that no longer exist; set them to N to remove them.

The tree updates itself when entities, devices, areas or labels change.

## Finding things {#search}

Type in the filter box to find a domain, device or entity by name or ID. The match ignores case and accents, and also spaces, dots, underscores and hyphens.

## {{label:selectBy.menu}} {#select-by}

Narrows the tree to one area, label or integration. It only changes what you see; it never grants anything. Choose **Reset** to show everything again.

## Entity hints {#hints}

A hint tells agents something about one entity, such as which lamp it is. **{{label:perms.addHint}}** appears on entities set to R, W or D.

Choose whether the hint is for this key only or for all keys, type up to 200 characters, and select **Save**. Saving empty text removes the hint. A key's own hint takes priority over one for all keys.

Hints are advice and never grant access. Agents and their model providers receive them, so never put secrets in a hint. Setting the entity back to N deletes this key's own hint for it.

## MESA profiles {#mesa-link}

The **+** or **MESA** button on a row opens the MESA profile for that domain, device or entity.

Related: [MESA](guide:workspace.mesa)

## {{label:workspace.clearAllPermissions}} {#clear-all}

**{{label:workspace.clearAllPermissions}}** on the toolbar removes every grant from this key, after you confirm. It also deletes this key's own hints; hints for all keys stay.

## Pass-through keys {#pass-through}

A pass-through key doesn't use the tree. **{{label:accessKeys.switchToScoped}}** turns the tree back on for it, straight away.

Related: [What pass-through opens](guide:topic.passThrough)
